Dear Dr. NerdLove:
I just read a post about a couple dealing with high libido – low libido compatibility, where the low libido partner has decided to just stop having sex with his partner and I felt … related.

I’ve been struggling with the same issues with my partner, we’ve been in a relationship from more than 10 years, but I’ve always had lower libido than her. So much lower, than she claims that she’s the only that initiates sex, and she’s probably right. I can go months without having sex, right now I think we’re approaching two years since the last time we have done it.

I feel awful about it, I think she’s very pretty and attractive, we both have gained weight throughout the years, and I’m completely aware that I’m at fault for the lack of sex… Yet, I don’t miss it. A couple years ago, fed up with my inactions, she told me if I ever wanted to have sex again it’s up to me, she’s done asking and begging… Only to keep telling me that I’m at fault for not engaging.
So, I was not given a choice. I was told, it’s up to me to have sex, and when I don’t, I’m still at fault for not doing so.

Recently I told her, it’s me completely me who doesn’t want to have sex, but she needs it. Needs it. She wants to have sex, and it kills me not being able to give her the one thing she wants of me. I’ve always struggled to make her cum, to satisfy her, I have countless times finish, go to the bathroom to clean me up and toss the condom only to hear her use her vibrator and finish. I hate being unable to make her feel good, I hate it.

Probably that’s why I stopped trying, I’m not good enough. If I could just caress and take her of her that would be fine, but lately I can’t even kiss her or hug her, how does she want me to have sex if I can’t even kiss her? I don’t even know anymore… I know it’s all my fault, I wish I was a better partner for her.
There’s so many things I’m not covering, I just don’t know where to even begin. I know I’m making myself the victim, I’m not without blame, I just don’t know anymore.
Too Much, Too Little, Too Late?

Let me ask you something TMTL2: have you two talked about this disconnect in your sex lives? And when I say “talked” I don’t mean the confrontation you mention, but actually sat down and had an Awkward Conversation about sex and intimacy in your relationship?

What I’m seeing in your letter is something I see in a lot of situations that are like yours: people who aren’t actually communicating with one another. They’re talking at, but not talking with, and certainly not talking about what they could do to try to accommodate each other without making demands that would be too much for one or the other.

And that’s assuming that they talk about it at all instead of just… well, apparently stewing in their emotions about it.
There’re a lot of factors that can affect a couple’s sex lives, starting just the longevity of the relationship. You and your partner have been together for more than a decade; it’s not exactly a surprise that there’s been a change in the frequency of sex in your relationship. Humans are a novelty-seeking species, and we’re incredibly adaptable; we can get used to almost literally anything. When we’re with the same partner for years at a time, we don’t produce as much dopamine and oxytocin during sex as we did at the start, when everything was new and novel.

That doesn’t mean that every relationship is doomed to become increasingly sexless; it just means that it takes effort to maintain levels of novelty and excitement as opposed to the early days when it’s so much easier.
But to get to that point, first it’s important to really dig into the situation and understand yourself and your partner.

If we take a step back for a moment, I think there’re a couple things going on here. The first is a question of libido. If you were to be perfectly honest with me, without fear of judgement, how would you describe your feelings about your sex drive? Is your lack of interest in sex something that bothers you for its own sake – that is, you would like to want sex more – or would this not be a problem for you if it wasn’t a problem for your partner? I would also ask if you’ve ever explored whether you have a more spontaneous arousal pattern – the classic “boner out of nowhere” type that’s common in men – or a responsive arousal pattern, where arousal starts after you start having sex.

These are be important questions to answer, because it’s going to affect how to proceed with trying to fix this relationship. If, for example, you are bothered by your lack of interest in sex, then it might not be a bad idea to go to a doctor and ask about getting some tests; there might be hormonal or other medical issues going on under the hood. Similarly, if part of the reason why you don’t initiate sex is because you don’t have a spontaneous arousal pattern, then part of the problem is that you’re treating sex as something that’s supposed to just happen. If you have more of a responsive arousal pattern, then part of the answer is to focus more on initiating intimacy – even if it’s just kissing, holding each other and engaging in some light making out – than to wait until the Erection Fairy remembers your address.

But if it really is the case that your problem isn’t that you lack an interest in sex, it’s how it affects your relationship… well, it’s possible that you’re one of those people who fall on the asexuality spectrum, where sexual desire just isn’t really a thing for you. If that’s the case, then the way to approach the issue would obviously be different.

But this leads to the second question: have you actually talked to your partner about what you want and need during sex? Have you talked with her about your different libidos and discussed options for meeting each other’s needs in ways that don’t make one of you feel neglected or exploited? Have you talked about any of the feelings that may come up for the two of you with this disconnect in your libidos? Does she feel disconnected to you or rejected by you? Do you feel pressured by her? Have you even talked about things that bother you or affect you with regards to sex that aren’t just about initiating or how much sex you are or aren’t having? I feel like there’s so much going unsaid here that by the time you’re talking about sex, you’re mostly arguing and blaming rather than problem solving.

You two are partners in this relationship, and that means that you’re supposed to be working together towards the common goal of supporting your relationship. You’re supposedly in this together; not talking, not exploring and not working with each other is the literal opposite of what you should be doing. It creates a wedge between you, driving you further apart when you should be looking for ways to bring yourselves together.

Let’s take how you feel like you can’t make your partner cum and you can hear her using a vibrator on herself after you’ve finished. While I understand that this makes you feel inadequate, this doesn’t mean that you’re incapable of pleasing her. What it means is that what your partner needs in order to orgasm is a sort of pressure, contact and sensation that is very difficult to achieve during penetration. That doesn’t make you a failure, it simply means that your partner is one of the 79% of the female population that can’t orgasm through penetration alone (and 44% can’t reach orgasm through penetration at all). Thus, the vibrator coming out after you’ve finished.

But here’s the thing: the fact that she needs the vibrator to get off doesn’t mean that you can’t please her, it means that you’re not using the tools she needs. If she needs direct and intense clitoral stimulation, then there’s no reason why you can’t be the person holding the vibrator. You have hands, after all; you could ask your wife to show you how she likes to use it and then use it on her when you have sex. You could make it part of the foreplay, you could even use it during penetration. The fact that you’re not giving her a look-ma-no-hands orgasm isn’t a strike against you as a lover; if anything, a willingness to incorporate sex toys is part of what makes someone a better lover. If you wouldn’t shame someone for using a hammer to build a home instead of pounding the nails in with their bare fists, you should be able to wrap your head around using a sex toy on and with your partner. It’s the hand that wields the tool that’s important, not the tool itself.

But that’s my point: you took this on as a sign of failure instead of going to your partner and saying “hey, is this something we could do to make sex better for you?” This sense of defeat could have been avoided if you had talked to her instead of just silently soaking in shame.

And here’s the thing that I think you’re missing: sex in a relationship isn’t just about orgasms, it’s about intimacy and connection. Right now, that’s a big part of what’s lacking for the both of you. There’s no intimacy, not because you won’t initiate, but because you two haven’t discussed what this means or what you could do about it. You haven’t tried to find compromises or ways of helping each other out. While I don’t feel like someone should be having sex that they don’t want, in a relationship we do have an obligation to our partners as well as to ourselves. While you may not feel like having sex, thereare other ways you can help your partner without actual sex. Giving her a masturbatory assist, for example, can help maintain that sense of intimacy and connection, even if it’s in the form of your holding her or making out with her while she masturbates or you use her vibrator on her. Other times, you two can have cuddles and connection without the pressure of an expectation that this would lead to sex when you’re not in the mood.
But as I said: this requires that the two of you have these conversations with one another, and it doesn’t sound like you’re doing that.

Besides doing your due diligence on your own health and sexuality, I think the best thing you could do for yourselves and this relationship is to find a sex-positive couple’s counselor and have a mediator help walk you through an Awkward Conversation about your sex life. At this point, I suspect that you’re going to want a trained third party who can help facilitate the conversation and ease you through the resentment and bitterness that’s clearly been building up between you. And I want to emphasize that you want a counselor who isn’t going to treat your partner’s libido as the problem or sex as something that should either be endured or as something that one party should be able to go without. If you don’t have one already or know where to find one, the American Association of Sex Educators, Counselors and Therapists has a referral directory that can help you find a counselor in your area.
https://s3-us-west-1.amazonaws.com/widget-images/become-patron-widget-medium%402x.png

Don’t look at going to a counselor as a failure on anyone’s part; look at it as getting help from a specialist to fix an issue in your relationship – no different than taking your car to the mechanic when it’s not running properly. While it would’ve been better to bring it in sooner, taking it in now can help make the difference between getting it back in working order… or realizing that you’ve passed the point of no return and there’s no way to fix things.
Good luck.
Hi Dr NerdLove,
I may be a little pessimistic at the moment, as I have just started university, but I feel like I won’t be loved.

I’ve had a few crushes in the past, and have tried hard to show that I deeply care for them, and have been honest about my feelings to them, but I am rejected every single time. I will admit, I’m not the best at flirting, but I’ve always tried to fill that gap with things that I am good at, like making gifts or writing poems. For instance, my current crush was diagnosed with cancer. During his entire treatment, I’ve kept in touch with him, made him a crotchet cat to keep him company and I got all our friends to write him get well soon notes which I turned into colourful origami roses. Of course, I never expected him to fall in love with me over it, but I sometimes selfishly feel like I deserve something. It’s a horrible thing to expect, and I hate myself for it.

I’m not very beautiful or attractive either. I’ve tried to fix that, but while I was, I’d gotten Crohn’s disease (essentially my immune system decided that there was something wrong with my gut when nothing was wrong, and has been attacking it) and as a consequence I was put on steroids to deal with it, and have gained even more weight. I’m still trying to lose it, but it just feels fruitless at this point in time, especially when I noticed girls who are of similar or heavier weights than me having incredible relationships.

I have dealt with a very long, depressive episode in my life for about 6 years (mostly because none of the staff at my school took me seriously) but I am better now thanks to the crush I mentioned above with cancer (which is probably the reason I’m struggling to get over him, since he has made a massive impact in my life). I managed to survive the years where I was alone mainly with the help of physics (ironically an existential crisis helped me realise that what I was going through was just a moment in time, which helped me gain some patience when it came to dealing with it) but annoying I didn’t spend much time expanding my area of interest. I am now, but I currently have such little amount of cultural knowledge that I find it hard to talk about anything apart from physics and mental health.

A good friend of mine has said to make a beautiful garden, and eventually the butterflies will come, but I’m getting rather impatient. I’m someone who loves physical connection, especially cuddling, holding hands and being patted on the head. I’m craving those feelings of warmth and safety, and I have no idea how to fill that void, especially when I’ve started a new chapter of my life.
Thank you for your time
Constant Cravings

Let’s start with the obvious: it’s not selfish to wish to be loved, CC, and wishing that your efforts were rewarded doesn’t make you a bad person. Your feelings aren’t what define you, even if those feelings seem unpleasant or ugly. Feelings just are; what you do with them and because of them is what makes the difference. It’s also important to remember that there’s a very significant difference between desiring something and feeling like you’re owed it. You didn’t support your crush because you expected something in return, you supported him because you care, you have compassion and empathy and you wanted to help him through a dark and scary time. The fact that there was a part of you that thought “…and I would love it if this lead to something” just means that you’re human, with human longings, same as the rest of us.
And I think you should understand that you are loved, CC. It’s not love in the way that you’re expecting or hoping for, but it is love and it is important. But we’ll get to that in a moment.

Instead, I want to say that your friend is right; cultivating a garden is how you attract the butterflies, and that’s something you should be doing. But I think one thing that’s important to remember is that taking care of yourself is part of that. You’re the garden after all; it doesn’t do you any good to be planting seeds when the soil itself needs to be tended to first.
https://www.doctornerdlove.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/shutterstock_1721152858.jpg

…ok, this metaphor is about a hairsbreadth away from going out of control. Let’s get less poetic and more frank: what are you doing to take care of yourself, physically, mentally and emotionally? What are you doing to help put yourself in a place where you’re able to give love freely and be able to receive it from others?

This isn’t an idle or rhetorical question; it’s a reminder that sometimes the love of your life needs to start with the love of your life. It’s much easier to find and accept love when you aren’t fighting against feelings of worthlessness or despair, when you aren’t asking people to love you despiteyourself. And it starts with loving yourself enough to try to make things better.

That’s going to start with addressing your health – mental as well as physical. One thing I would suggest is to start with talking to your doctor about your treatment for your Crohn’s disease. While there aren’t any treatments that have no side-effects, it is worth talking to your doctor about possible alternatives that strike a balance between effectiveness and safety. You are fully within your rights to advocate for yourself when the side-effects of a treatment are negatively interfering in your life – even if the interference is making you feel bad about yourself. Corticosteroids aren’t intended for long-term maintenance, so it may be good to talk to your doctor about when and how you’re going to be tapered off and what other options you could pursue. There are a number of biologics that focus more on the immune response as the inflammation, that target inflammatory pathways or that help bring Crohn’s into remission.

At the same time, I would recommend talking to a psychiatrist about getting an antidepressant in combination with therapy. While it’s great that supporting your friend through his cancer helped (and it says amazing things about you as a person and as a friend), that’s not really the same as treatment. Taking care of others to take care of yourself runs the risk of burning yourself out as it tends to come with diminishing returns – especially if it gets tangled up with complex or uncomfortable feelings about deservedness or reciprocity. Taking care of yourself by seeking effective treatment isn’t being selfish; it’s caring about yourself so that you have the resources to be able to care for others as well.

Of course, considering that you’re already medically complex, it would be vitally important that you ensure that both your endocrinologist and psychiatrist (or whomever you turn to for an antidepressant) knows about your condition and how it’s being treated.

The next thing I would recommend is to look to your friends for support. It sounds like you have a fairly robust social circle of people who love and care for you, as you’ve loved and cared for them. Have you asked them for support and connection? Have you looked to them for the possibility of that warmth and safety you’re missing, even possibly for platonic cuddles and physical affection? Love, after all, comes in many forms besides eros; agape (selfless love), philia (the love of close friends) and storge (the love of family) are all just as real and important. While it may not be the same as the sort of love you might have hoped for from your crush, it still helps fill that need and – importantly – helps build the foundation of that garden that will enable other forms of love to grow. Having many forms of love in your life helps bring more love to you; it increases your capacity to accept love while giving you greater ability to give love away… which in turn brings more in.

This is also true for broadening your cultural horizons. If you’re at a point where you have relatively little cultural knowledge, then now is a great time to seek it out with the help of your friends. Here’s the thing that we often forget: people love to share their cultural knowledge with others. There’re few things that feel better than introducing someone new to something that we love; just ask any fan of a particular genre, tv series, book series, movie, author or musical artist. Turning to your friends and saying “Hey, I don’t know a lot about $THEIR_PARTICULAR_INTEREST, do you have any recommendations?” is going to be like giving them a gift. If anything, you might have to prepare yourself for a deluge of options to explore, because many of them will turn on the firehose if they’re not careful.

It’s also a good time to get intellectually curious and explore things yourself, for the sake of figuring out what your tastes are and where your interests lie. Since you’re entering university, now is a great time to take advantage of the options that are being presented to you – whether it’s on-campus events, lectures, extracurricular activities, clubs and more. Maybe now is an opportunity to discover that you love doing improv and theater. Or maybe you’ll find that you’re into spoken word poetry or discover a Makerspace and be inspired. Not everything is going to be your particular flavor and that’s ok, because you’re still going to be learning what you do and don’t vibe with. That’s part of learning and growing.

Now you may notice that these are all about you and your personal development and growth, not necessarily about finding love. But that’s the thing: this isn’t just about laying the groundwork, it’s about increasing the surface area for love to attach. Exploring your world, engaging your intellectual curiosity, bonding and deepening that bond with your friends are all ways that you not only put yourself in love’s path but increase the ways and opportunities for love to enter your life. It also is engaging you – helping bring passion, curiosity, contentment and satisfaction into your life. Like hiding vegetables under a delicious blanket of melted cheese or a pill in peanut butter, this helps you build that garden you mentioned while tempering and easing that sense of impatience. You’re doing things that engage you, occupy you and satisfy you, helping change your focus away from time to simply enjoying the journey you’re on.

And that, more than anything else, is going to be what helps you find love. It’s following the hoary cliché of “it’ll happen when you least expect it”, by putting you in places where you’re not expecting it simply because you have so much going on that you also love. It helps open you up to serendipity, simply because you are putting yourself out there in more ways, meeting more people, making more connections and doing so in a way that doesn’t feel like work or struggle. It just feels like… living your life. And a good life at that. A life that is already enriching and fulfilling and will be complemented by sharing it with someone else, instead of completed.

I know things feel dark and empty right now and that when you look around, you just see the event horizon of despair. But I promise you: no matter how depth and dark the night, the sun always returns, and hope shines bright.
All will be well.

While it would’ve been better to bring it in sooner, taking it in now can help make the difference between getting it back in working order… or realizing that you’ve passed the point of no return and there’s no way to fix things.

Good luck.

Constant Cravings

Let’s start with the obvious: it’s not selfish to wish to be loved, CC, and wishing that your efforts were rewarded doesn’t make you a bad person. Your feelings aren’t what define you, even if those feelings seem unpleasant or ugly. Feelings just are; what you do with them and because of them is what makes the difference. It’s also important to remember that there’s a very significant difference between desiring something and feeling like you’re owed it. You didn’t support your crush because you expected something in return, you supported him because you care, you have compassion and empathy and you wanted to help him through a dark and scary time. The fact that there was a part of you that thought “…and I would love it if this lead to something” just means that you’re human, with human longings, same as the rest of us.

And I think you should understand that you are loved, CC. It’s not love in the way that you’re expecting or hoping for, but it is love and it is important. But we’ll get to that in a moment.

Instead, I want to say that your friend is right; cultivating a garden is how you attract the butterflies, and that’s something you should be doing. But I think one thing that’s important to remember is that taking care of yourself is part of that. You’re the garden after all; it doesn’t do you any good to be planting seeds when the soil itself needs to be tended to first.

…ok, this metaphor is about a hairsbreadth away from going out of control. Let’s get less poetic and more frank: what are you doing to take care of yourself, physically, mentally and emotionally? What are you doing to help put yourself in a place where you’re able to give love freely and be able to receive it from others?

This isn’t an idle or rhetorical question; it’s a reminder that sometimes the love of your life needs to start with the love of your life. It’s much easier to find and accept love when you aren’t fighting against feelings of worthlessness or despair, when you aren’t asking people to love you despiteyourself. And it starts with loving yourself enough to try to make things better.

That’s going to start with addressing your health – mental as well as physical. One thing I would suggest is to start with talking to your doctor about your treatment for your Crohn’s disease. While there aren’t any treatments that have no side-effects, it is worth talking to your doctor about possible alternatives that strike a balance between effectiveness and safety. You are fully within your rights to advocate for yourself when the side-effects of a treatment are negatively interfering in your life – even if the interference is making you feel bad about yourself. Corticosteroids aren’t intended for long-term maintenance, so it may be good to talk to your doctor about when and how you’re going to be tapered off and what other options you could pursue. There are a number of biologics that focus more on the immune response as the inflammation, that target inflammatory pathways or that help bring Crohn’s into remission.

At the same time, I would recommend talking to a psychiatrist about getting an antidepressant in combination with therapy. While it’s great that supporting your friend through his cancer helped (and it says amazing things about you as a person and as a friend), that’s not really the same as treatment. Taking care of others to take care of yourself runs the risk of burning yourself out as it tends to come with diminishing returns – especially if it gets tangled up with complex or uncomfortable feelings about deservedness or reciprocity. Taking care of yourself by seeking effective treatment isn’t being selfish; it’s caring about yourself so that you have the resources to be able to care for others as well.

Of course, considering that you’re already medically complex, it would be vitally important that you ensure that both your endocrinologist and psychiatrist (or whomever you turn to for an antidepressant) knows about your condition and how it’s being treated.

The next thing I would recommend is to look to your friends for support. It sounds like you have a fairly robust social circle of people who love and care for you, as you’ve loved and cared for them. Have you asked them for support and connection? Have you looked to them for the possibility of that warmth and safety you’re missing, even possibly for platonic cuddles and physical affection? Love, after all, comes in many forms besides eros; agape (selfless love), philia (the love of close friends) and storge (the love of family) are all just as real and important. While it may not be the same as the sort of love you might have hoped for from your crush, it still helps fill that need and – importantly – helps build the foundation of that garden that will enable other forms of love to grow. Having many forms of love in your life helps bring more love to you; it increases your capacity to accept love while giving you greater ability to give love away… which in turn brings more in.

This is also true for broadening your cultural horizons. If you’re at a point where you have relatively little cultural knowledge, then now is a great time to seek it out with the help of your friends. Here’s the thing that we often forget: people love to share their cultural knowledge with others. There’re few things that feel better than introducing someone new to something that we love; just ask any fan of a particular genre, tv series, book series, movie, author or musical artist. Turning to your friends and saying “Hey, I don’t know a lot about $THEIR_PARTICULAR_INTEREST, do you have any recommendations?” is going to be like giving them a gift. If anything, you might have to prepare yourself for a deluge of options to explore, because many of them will turn on the firehose if they’re not careful.

It’s also a good time to get intellectually curious and explore things yourself, for the sake of figuring out what your tastes are and where your interests lie. Since you’re entering university, now is a great time to take advantage of the options that are being presented to you – whether it’s on-campus events, lectures, extracurricular activities, clubs and more. Maybe now is an opportunity to discover that you love doing improv and theater. Or maybe you’ll find that you’re into spoken word poetry or discover a Makerspace and be inspired. Not everything is going to be your particular flavor and that’s ok, because you’re still going to be learning what you do and don’t vibe with. That’s part of learning and growing.

Now you may notice that these are all about you and your personal development and growth, not necessarily about finding love. But that’s the thing: this isn’t just about laying the groundwork, it’s about increasing the surface area for love to attach. Exploring your world, engaging your intellectual curiosity, bonding and deepening that bond with your friends are all ways that you not only put yourself in love’s path but increase the ways and opportunities for love to enter your life. It also is engaging you – helping bring passion, curiosity, contentment and satisfaction into your life. Like hiding vegetables under a delicious blanket of melted cheese or a pill in peanut butter, this helps you build that garden you mentioned while tempering and easing that sense of impatience. You’re doing things that engage you, occupy you and satisfy you, helping change your focus away from time to simply enjoying the journey you’re on.

And that, more than anything else, is going to be what helps you find love. It’s following the hoary cliché of “it’ll happen when you least expect it”, by putting you in places where you’re not expecting it simply because you have so much going on that you also love. It helps open you up to serendipity, simply because you are putting yourself out there in more ways, meeting more people, making more connections and doing so in a way that doesn’t feel like work or struggle. It just feels like… living your life. And a good life at that. A life that is already enriching and fulfilling and will be complemented by sharing it with someone else, instead of completed.

I know things feel dark and empty right now and that when you look around, you just see the event horizon of despair. But I promise you: no matter how depth and dark the night, the sun always returns, and hope shines bright.

All will be well.
